findings.headline: Health care and social assistance is the largest private employer here, at 37.0% of jobs

findings.why_it_matters: an economy's exposure runs through whatever drives demand for its largest sectors. A county concentrated in one sector rises and falls with it, and a county spread across many has a different problem -- no sector large enough to anchor a supply chain.
findings.question_that_follows: what sustains demand for health care and social assistance here, and does that demand come from inside this county or from outside it?
qualifications: private employer establishments only
a share of employment is not a share of output or of value added
findings.not_an_investment_claim: this describes an economy. It does not identify an investment, and nothing here establishes that money put into it would earn a return.

findings.headline: Construction carries 17.7% of the payroll on 14.0% of the jobs

findings.why_it_matters: household income depends on how large the high-paying sectors are, not on how large the economy is. A county can add jobs and not add earnings, and the sector mix is what decides which happens.
findings.question_that_follows: is the size of construction here set by local demand, or by an institution, a programme or a market outside this county?
qualifications: payroll per employee is not a wage: it mixes full-time, part-time and seasonal work
CBP payroll excludes employer-paid benefits
findings.not_an_investment_claim: this describes an economy. It does not identify an investment, and nothing here establishes that money put into it would earn a return.

findings.headline: the average establishment here employs 5.1 people

findings.why_it_matters: average firm size bounds what any single firm can finance, absorb or expand into without outside capital. It also decides whether a development conversation has one counterparty or two hundred.
findings.question_that_follows: is there any firm here large enough to be a counterparty for a development or supply agreement, and who are they?
qualifications: CBP publishes establishments, not firms: several may share an owner, and ownership is not published
an average says nothing about the distribution
findings.not_an_investment_claim: this describes an economy. It does not identify an investment, and nothing here establishes that money put into it would earn a return.

findings.headline: 9 establishments opened and 4 closed in 2023

findings.why_it_matters: whether an economy grows by forming firms or by existing firms expanding decides which development lever applies. Entrepreneur support and incumbent expansion are different programmes with different costs.
findings.question_that_follows: is the net change here formation or expansion, and which of the two is the constraint?
qualifications: BDS uses a different frame from CBP, so its establishment counts are not CBP's
entry and exit are establishment events, not firm events
findings.not_an_investment_claim: this describes an economy. It does not identify an investment, and nothing here establishes that money put into it would earn a return.

findings.headline: the employment data shows 0 agricultural jobs; the agricultural census counts 501 farm operations

agricultural census sales are gross receipts, not earnings

at_a_glance.headline: This economy employs 292 people in 7 private sectors, in 57 establishments, paying $9,865,000 a year. Dula measures that structure. What it has INVESTIGATED is the food system within it.
at_a_glance.structure: Dula has IDENTIFIED 11 buyer-side and 5 producer-side actors here, in a research population built by the food study. That is the shape of the inventory, not of the economy: whether this place buys more food than it produces would need production, consumption, procurement and trade evidence, and none of the four is held.
at_a_glance.strongest_evidence: employment and earnings, commuting, 18 named actors, 195 observations
at_a_glance.weakest: capital deployment, procurement relationships, ownership, firm revenues and margins — all unmeasured
at_a_glance.prior_sentence: Mora functions as a place people live and work somewhere else within New Mexico: 67.2% of its working residents work outside the county, most of them in San Miguel. Average private earnings at workplaces here are $3,984 a month. 10.84% of its workers travel 60 minutes or more, against 6.8% statewide. Median rent is $887 against a median household income of $53,663. Observed here: labour relationships, population and age structure, housing stock, tenure and cost burden. Not observed: local capital deployment, procurement relationships.
at_a_glance.why_it_changed: the page previously opened with the commuting sentence because LODES is the most complete dataset held, not because commuting is the most important thing about this economy

findings.headline: Accommodation and food services is the largest private employer here, at 25.2% of jobs

findings.why_it_matters: an economy's exposure runs through whatever drives demand for its largest sectors. A county concentrated in one sector rises and falls with it, and a county spread across many has a different problem -- no sector large enough to anchor a supply chain.
findings.question_that_follows: what sustains demand for accommodation and food services here, and does that demand come from inside this county or from outside it?
qualifications: private employer establishments only
a share of employment is not a share of output or of value added

findings.headline: Health care and social assistance carries 24.5% of the payroll on 18.4% of the jobs

an average says nothing about the distribution
